generatedBy.purpose: Reduce human sense-selection and child-definition drafting effort; suggestions remain unreviewed.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: An answer is what you say or write when someone asks you a question.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: Riya raised her hand and gave the answer.
suggestions.rationale: The reply-to-a-question sense is the ordinary early-primary noun; solution/result and speech-act readings are more specialized.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: A door is a movable panel that opens and closes an entrance.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: Please close the door when you leave.
suggestions.rationale: The physical barrier is the concrete child-facing meaning; doorway-space and figurative access readings are secondary.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: Difficult means not easy and needing extra effort.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: The last puzzle was difficult, but Maya kept trying.
suggestions.rationale: The general not-easy sense is foundational; hard-to-control is a narrower second reading.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: A century is a period of one hundred years.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: One century is the same as 100 years.
suggestions.rationale: The time-period sense is the standard school meaning; the bare numerical-hundred sense is secondary.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: An eye is the body part that helps you see.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: She covered one eye during the vision test.
suggestions.rationale: The organ-of-sight sense is concrete and foundational; discernment and attention readings are figurative.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: Often means many times or frequently.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: We often read a story before bed.
suggestions.rationale: Frequent recurrence is the ordinary child-facing adverb reading.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: New means recently made, found, bought, or begun.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: Aarav brought a new notebook to school.
suggestions.rationale: Candidate 3 is the ordinary recently-created/acquired sense; candidates 1 and 2 are historical-language senses.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: Good means having qualities that are useful, pleasant, or right for what is needed.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: This is a good book for beginning readers.
suggestions.rationale: The broad positive-quality sense is the safest general classroom reading; full-measure and specifically moral readings are narrower.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: First means coming before all the others.
suggestions.rationale: Ordering in time or space is the foundational child meaning; musical-rank and opening-only readings are narrower.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: To believe something means to accept that it is true.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: I believe your story because you told me what happened.
suggestions.rationale: Accept-as-true is the ordinary base meaning; regard/judge and confidence readings are related but distinct.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: Work is effort or activity used to make or do something.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: Cleaning the garden took a lot of work.
suggestions.rationale: Activity or effort is the broad foundational noun; product and paid-employment senses are distinct.

suggestions.proposedChildDefinition: Best means having the most positive qualities among the choices.
suggestions.proposedChildExample: She chose the best picture for the poster.
suggestions.rationale: The superlative-of-good sense is the ordinary child-facing adjective; most-advisable is narrower.
